pages.title: About RacerX
pages.body:
RacerX is a serverless, cloud-synced collaboration platform for small teams and businesses. It gives your team real database and application power — without servers, without IT, and without recurring subscription fees.

Everything your team creates lives in your own cloud storage account (Dropbox and OneDrive supported; Box and Google Drive coming). RacerX never stores your data on its own servers. You own your data completely.

**What makes RacerX different:**

Most team tools — Slack, Teams, Notion — are SaaS products. Your data lives on someone else's servers, and you pay every month to access it. If you stop paying, you lose access. RacerX works differently. Your workspace is a folder in your cloud storage. Your data is yours. RacerX is just the app that reads and writes it.

**What RacerX includes:**

- **RacerX Messenger** — team chat with channels and Markdown message formatting
- **RacerX Wiki** — a team knowledge base with rich WYSIWYG editing, categories, pages, embedded SQL reports, and PDF export
- **RacerX Forms Apps** — structured database apps (CRM, issue tracker, and more) with list view, kanban, record editing, CSV import/export, and sortable/resizable columns
- **SQL Viewer** — query your RacerX data directly using SQL, or describe what you want in plain English and let the AI generate the query
- **RacerX Platform** — the underlying sync engine that powers everything

pages.title: How RacerX Works
pages.body:
RacerX stores all data as JSON files in your cloud storage. Each message, wiki page, form record, and channel is a single file. The app polls cloud storage on a regular schedule, downloads new files, and stores them in a local SQLite database on your device. The UI reads from that local database — so everything is fast and works offline.

**The sync cycle:**

1. You send a message, save a wiki page, or edit a form record
2. RacerX writes it to local SQLite immediately (you see it instantly)
3. RacerX uploads a JSON file to cloud storage in the background
4. Other team members' apps poll cloud storage, find the new file, download it, and write it to their local SQLite
5. Their UI refreshes automatically

**Polling intervals:**

- Messenger: checks for new content every 15 seconds when the app is in the foreground; every 5 minutes in the background
- Wiki: checks every 5 minutes when the app is in the foreground
- Forms: checks every 5 minutes when the app is in the foreground
- The app checks immediately when you switch back to it from another app

**Conflict resolution:**

If two people edit the same record at the same time, the most recent save wins. This is called "last write wins."

**Your files in the cloud:**

RacerX uploads and downloads files directly via the cloud provider's API. Your RacerX data does not pass through or get cached in your local Dropbox or OneDrive folder — you will not see it there. To browse your RacerX files directly, use the cloud provider's web interface (dropbox.com or onedrive.live.com) and navigate to the RacerX folder.

pages.title: System Requirements
pages.body:
| Platform | Minimum Version |
|---|---|
| macOS | macOS 12 Monterey or later |
| Windows | Windows 10 (version 1903) or later |
| iOS | Coming soon |
| Android | Coming soon |

RacerX requires an active cloud storage account. A free Dropbox or OneDrive account is sufficient for getting started.

**No desktop client required:**

RacerX communicates directly with cloud storage through the provider's API. You do not need to install the Dropbox desktop app or the OneDrive desktop app — RacerX handles all file transfers itself. Your RacerX data will not appear in your local Dropbox or OneDrive sync folder; use the provider's website to browse files if needed.

pages.title: Signing In
pages.body:
RacerX uses your cloud storage account for authentication. You do not create a separate RacerX account — your cloud storage account is your identity.

**First launch:**

1. Open RacerX
2. Click **Sign in with Dropbox** (or the appropriate cloud storage provider)
3. Your browser will open to an authorization page
4. Review the permissions and click **Allow**
5. Your browser will redirect back to RacerX automatically
6. RacerX will display your workspaces or prompt you to create one

**Security:**

Your cloud storage credentials are never seen by RacerX. Authentication happens entirely through the cloud provider's OAuth system. RacerX stores your access token securely in your device's keychain (macOS) or credential store (Windows).

**Signing out:**

Click your cloud provider icon in the bottom-left of the sidebar to open the account panel, then click **Sign out**. When you sign out, all local session data is cleared. Your cloud data is never deleted.

pages.title: Workspaces
pages.body:
A workspace is a shared folder in your cloud storage that your team uses together. Each workspace has its own set of apps — Messenger channels, Wiki pages, Forms apps, and more.

**Creating a new workspace:**

1. After signing in, click **Workspaces** in the left sidebar
2. Click **Create New Workspace**
3. Enter a workspace name
4. RacerX creates the folder structure in your cloud storage
5. You are taken to the main app with your new workspace selected

**Switching workspaces:**

Click **Workspaces** at the top of the sidebar to open the workspace browser. Click any workspace in the list to switch to it.

**Multiple workspaces:**

You can belong to multiple workspaces — for example, one for your full team and one for a specific project. Each workspace is independent; switching between them updates the entire app.

**Inviting team members:**

Workspace owners can share the workspace folder through the cloud provider's sharing interface. The person you invite will see the shared workspace on their next launch of RacerX.

pages.title: Navigating the App
pages.body:
RacerX is organized around a left sidebar and a tabbed main area.

**Left sidebar:**

The sidebar shows your current workspace and provides access to all apps. Click any app in the sidebar to open it. You can collapse the sidebar to a narrow strip by clicking the **‹** button at the top — click **›** to expand it again.

**Tabs:**

Each open app appears as a tab at the top of the main area. The fixed tabs are always present:

- **Messenger** — team chat
- **Wiki** — knowledge base
- **Guide** — this guide (read-only)
- **SQL Viewer** — direct database query tool

Forms apps appear as additional tabs. Close a tab using the **×** on the tab.

**Opening a Forms app:**

Click the app name in the sidebar to open it in a new tab (or switch to its existing tab if already open).

**Switching between apps:**

Click any tab at the top, or click an app in the sidebar.

pages.title: Using RacerX Messenger
pages.body:
Messenger is RacerX's team chat. It works like a simple channel-based chat tool.

**Channels:**

Channels organize conversations by topic. The channel list appears in the left panel of the Messenger tab. To create a new channel, click the **+** icon next to **CHANNELS** in the panel header, enter a channel name, and click Create.

**Sending messages:**

Click a channel name to open it. Type in the compose bar at the bottom and press **Enter** or click **Send**.

Messages support **Markdown** formatting:
- `**bold**` → **bold**
- `*italic*` → *italic*
- `` `code` `` → `code`
- `# Heading`
- `- bullet list`

**Collapsing the channel list:**

Click the **‹** icon in the Messenger panel header to collapse the channel list to a narrow strip, giving the message thread more space. Click **›** to expand it again.

pages.title: Using the Wiki
pages.body:
The Wiki is your team's knowledge base. Use it for documentation, processes, onboarding guides, meeting notes, and embedded live reports.

**Structure:**

The Wiki is organized into **Categories** and **Pages**. Categories appear in the left panel with **+**/**−** toggles. Pages live inside categories. Click **−** next to a category to collapse it; click **+** to expand.

**Creating a new page:**

1. Click the **+** button in the Wiki panel header
2. Choose an existing category from the dropdown, or select **+ New category…** to create one
3. If creating a new category, enter the category name
4. Enter the page title
5. Click **Create**

The new page opens automatically and is ready to edit.

**Editing a page:**

Click a page name in the left panel to open it. The toolbar above the editor is active for editable wikis. Click in the content area and start typing. Changes are saved automatically about one second after you stop typing — the **Saved** indicator appears in the toolbar when the save completes.

**Collapsing the page list:**

Click the **‹** button in the Wiki panel header to collapse the left panel. Click **›** on the narrow strip to expand it again.

**The RacerX Guide:**

The Guide tab shows this guide. It uses the same wiki component as your team's wiki, but in read-only mode — the toolbar is not shown and pages cannot be edited.

pages.title: Wiki Editor — Formatting Toolbar
pages.body:
When you open a wiki page for editing, the formatting toolbar appears below the page title. It gives you full control over text formatting, structure, and content.

**Inline text formatting:**

| Button | Effect | Keyboard shortcut |
|---|---|---|
| **B** | Bold | ⌘B / Ctrl+B |
| *I* | Italic | ⌘I / Ctrl+I |
| ~~S~~ | Strikethrough | — |
| `` ` `` | Inline code | — |
| 🔗 | Link | — |

**Headings:**

- **H1**, **H2**, **H3** — click to turn the current paragraph into a heading at that level. Click the active heading button again to convert it back to body text.

**Lists:**

- **•≡** — bulleted list
- **1≡** — numbered list

Press **Enter** to add the next item. Press **Enter** twice on an empty item to exit the list.

**Block elements:**

- **❝** — Blockquote. Useful for highlighting important notes or quoting external content.
- **</>** — Code block. A full-width monospace block for multi-line code samples.
- **—** — Horizontal rule (dividing line).
- **⊞** — Insert a 3×3 table with a header row. Click in any cell to type. Add rows and columns by right-clicking inside the table.

**Edit history:**

- **↩** — Undo (⌘Z / Ctrl+Z)
- **↪** — Redo (⌘⇧Z / Ctrl+⇧Z)

**Save indicator:**

The right side of the toolbar shows the save state: **Saving…** while the auto-save is pending, **Saved** in green when the page has been written to cloud storage, or **Save failed** in red if a network error prevented saving.

**Bubble menu:**

When you select text, a small floating toolbar appears near the selection with the most common formatting options: Bold, Italic, Strikethrough, H1, H2. Use it for quick formatting without reaching for the main toolbar.

pages.title: Wiki Editor — Working with Links
pages.body:
To add a link to wiki page text:

1. Select the text you want to make into a link
2. Click the **🔗** button in the toolbar
3. A URL bar appears below the toolbar
4. Type or paste the URL (e.g. `https://example.com`)
5. Press **Enter** or click **Set**

The selected text becomes a link, styled in blue and underlined.

**Editing an existing link:**

Place the cursor anywhere inside a linked word or phrase, then click **🔗**. The URL bar opens pre-filled with the current URL. Edit the URL and click **Set**, or click **Remove** to strip the link formatting from the text (the text itself remains).

**Autolinking:**

If you type a full URL directly in the editor (e.g. `https://example.com`), the editor automatically converts it to a clickable link.

**Cancelling the link bar:**

Press **Escape** or click **Cancel** to dismiss the URL bar without making any changes.

pages.title: Wiki Editor — Tables
pages.body:
To insert a table into a wiki page:

1. Place the cursor where you want the table
2. Click the **⊞** button in the toolbar

A 3-column, 3-row table appears with the first row as a header. The table is styled with borders and the header row has a shaded background.

**Typing in a table:**

Click any cell and type. Press **Tab** to move to the next cell. Pressing Tab in the last cell of a row moves to the first cell of the next row. Pressing Tab in the very last cell adds a new row.

**Table formatting:**

Table cells support all inline formatting: bold, italic, inline code, links, and strikethrough. Headings and lists inside table cells are not supported.

**Selecting cells:**

Click and drag to select multiple cells. Selected cells are highlighted in light blue. You can apply formatting to the content of all selected cells at once.

**When to use tables:**

- Reference information with clear columns (e.g. command name, description, example)
- Feature comparison grids
- Configuration parameter lists

For data that changes frequently, consider using a **Report Block** instead — it pulls live data from your database every time the page loads.

pages.title: Wiki Editor — Code Blocks
pages.body:
A code block is a full-width section with a monospace font, distinct background, and preserved whitespace. Use it for multi-line code samples, terminal commands, configuration files, and any content where exact spacing and line breaks matter.

**Inserting a code block:**

- Click the **</>** button in the toolbar, or
- Start a new line and type three backticks (` ``` `) then press Enter

**Inline code vs. code blocks:**

Use **inline code** (`` ` `` button) for short fragments within a sentence — file names, command names, variable names, short snippets. Use a **code block** for multi-line samples that need their own visual block.

**SQL Report Blocks:**

A special code block variant — ` ```report ``` ` — executes a SQL query and renders the results as a live table inline in the page. See the **Wiki Report Blocks** page for full details.

pages.title: Wiki Report Blocks
pages.body:
A Report Block embeds a live SQL query directly in a wiki page. When the page is displayed, the query runs against your local database and the results appear as a table — inline with the rest of the page content. A single wiki page can contain multiple report blocks mixed with regular text.

This turns any wiki page into a live report that always reflects current data.

**Adding a report block:**

The easiest approach:
1. Open the **SQL Viewer** tab
2. Write and run a query to verify the results look correct
3. Click **Copy as Report** in the SQL Viewer header — this copies the query wrapped in the correct report block syntax, with table IDs automatically replaced by the `{app}` token
4. Open the wiki page you want to add it to and click in the editor
5. Paste (⌘V or Ctrl+V) — the report block appears immediately and runs the query

**What the report block looks like in the page body:**

````
```report
SELECT title FROM wiki_pages_{app} ORDER BY title
```
````

Three backticks followed by the word `report`, your SQL on the next line(s), then three closing backticks on their own line.

**Tokens:**

Report blocks use tokens as placeholders for app identifiers. This makes reports portable — the report works in any workspace without edits.

| Token | Resolves to |
|---|---|
| `{app}` | The current wiki's app ID |
| `{messenger}` | The workspace's Messenger app ID |
| `{me}` | Your own account id, as a quoted value — e.g. `WHERE created_by = {me}` shows only what you created |

The **Copy as Report** button in the SQL Viewer applies the correct token automatically. Use it rather than typing tokens by hand.

**Toggle the SQL:**

Each report block has a **+ SQL** toggle at the bottom. Click it to reveal the SQL source for that block. Click again to hide it.

**Report block errors:**

If a query fails, the block shows an inline error message instead of a result table. Common causes:
- The table name is wrong or the `{app}` token is missing
- A SQL syntax error
- Querying a Messenger table without using the `{messenger}` token

Open the SQL Viewer to test and correct the query, then paste the corrected block back in.

pages.title: Exporting the Wiki to PDF
pages.body:
You can export the entire wiki — all categories and pages — as a single PDF document.

**To export:**

1. In the Wiki left panel, click the **picture_as_pdf** icon (📄) in the panel header
2. A PDF is generated with a table of contents, all pages in category order, and consistent headers and footers
3. Your device's print/save dialog appears — choose **Save as PDF** or print directly

**What's included:**

- Table of contents with page numbers
- All categories and their pages, in the order shown in the left panel
- All text, headings, lists, tables, and code blocks
- Report blocks show their SQL source rather than live query results (since PDF is a static snapshot)

**Single-page printing:**

To print or export a single wiki page, select all text on the page and use your browser's print function. Full single-page PDF export with custom layout is on the roadmap.

pages.title: What Are Forms Apps?
pages.body:
Forms Apps are structured database applications built into RacerX. Each app stores records — rows of data with defined fields — and gives your team multiple ways to view and manage that data.

**Built-in app types:**

- **CRM** — Customer relationship management. Contains three apps: Contacts, Companies, and Pipeline. Use it to track prospects, deals, and client relationships.
- **Issue Tracker** — Bug and task tracking with status, priority, assignee, and description fields.
- **Kanban** — A flexible board-style app for any workflow.

**All Forms Apps include:**

- **List view** — a spreadsheet-style table with sortable, resizable, and reorderable columns
- **Kanban view** — a card-based view organized by status or another categorical field
- **Record panel** — a full side panel showing all fields for a selected record, with inline editing
- **CSV import and export** — bring data in from a spreadsheet or export your data at any time

**Where Forms Apps live:**

Forms Apps appear in the left sidebar under your workspace. Click an app name to open it in a new tab. The app syncs bidirectionally with cloud storage — changes you make are visible to other team members within 5 minutes.

pages.title: List View
pages.body:
The List View is the default view for all Forms Apps. It shows your records as rows in a table, one column per field.

**Opening a record:**

Click any row to open the **Record Panel** on the right side. The panel slides in and shows all fields for that record, and the row stays highlighted while it is open.

**Sorting:**

Click any column header to sort by that column. Click again to reverse the sort direction (ascending → descending → ascending).

**Resizing columns:**

Hover over the right edge of a column header — the cursor changes to a resize arrow. Click and drag to the left or right to change the column width. Release to set the new width.

**Reordering columns:**

Click and drag a column header to move it to a new position. When dragging, a drop indicator appears between columns showing where the column will land. Dragging near the left or right edge of the table automatically scrolls the table.

**Collapsing the sidebar:**

The secondary navigation panel (showing app sections or views) can be collapsed by clicking the **‹** icon in the panel header. Click **›** on the narrow strip to expand it again. This gives the list view more horizontal space.

**System columns:**

Every record includes system-managed metadata: record ID, created timestamp, last-updated timestamp, and the workspace ID. These columns appear after the data columns and cannot be edited.

pages.title: Record Panel
pages.body:
The Record Panel shows the full details of a single record. Open it by clicking any row in the List View.

**Resizing the panel:**

Drag the thin divider on the left edge of the panel to make it wider or narrower. The list view adjusts to fill the remaining space. Resize it as wide as you need to read long text fields.

**Viewing a record:**

All fields are displayed in the panel with their labels and current values. Lookup fields (such as **Assignee** or **Company**) show the resolved name rather than a raw ID.

**Editing a record:**

1. Click the **Edit** button in the panel header
2. Each field becomes editable:
   - **Short text fields** — single-line text input
   - **Long text fields** (more than a sentence) — multi-line textarea that grows as you type
   - **Lookup fields** (user, status, or linked-record fields) — a dropdown picklist showing all valid options
3. Click **Save** to write the changes, or **Cancel** to discard

Changes saved via the Record Panel are written immediately to local SQLite and queued for upload to cloud storage.

**Closing the panel:**

Click anywhere outside the panel, or click the **×** in the panel header.

pages.title: Kanban View
pages.body:
The Kanban View shows records as cards organized in vertical columns. Each column represents a value of the primary status or category field.

**Switching to Kanban:**

Click the **Kanban** toggle above the list view to switch. Click **List** to switch back.

**Cards:**

Each card shows the record's title field and key metadata. Click a card to open its Record Panel on the right.

**Columns:**

Columns correspond to the status field values defined in the app's schema. For example, an Issue Tracker Kanban might have columns: **Open**, **In Progress**, **Done**.

**When to use Kanban:**

Kanban is most useful for workflows where records move through stages — issue tracking, deal pipeline, onboarding tasks. Use List View when you need to see many records at once or compare values across columns.

pages.title: Import and Export
pages.body:
All Forms Apps support importing data from CSV files and exporting data to CSV.

**Exporting to CSV:**

1. Open the Forms App in List View
2. Click the **Export CSV** button in the app header
3. A CSV file is downloaded to your device
4. Open it in any spreadsheet application (Numbers, Excel, Google Sheets)

The export includes all visible fields in the current column order.

**Importing from CSV:**

1. Open the Forms App in List View
2. Click **Import CSV** in the app header
3. Select a CSV file from your device
4. Choose the import mode:
   - **Merge** — adds the imported records to existing records. Existing records are not changed.
   - **Replace** — replaces all existing records with the imported data. Previous records are permanently deleted.
5. Click **Import**

**CSV format:**

The first row of the CSV must be a header row. Column names must match the field names defined in the app's schema. Columns in the CSV that do not match any field are ignored. Fields in the schema that are not in the CSV are left blank on imported records.

**Tips:**

- Export first to get a correctly formatted CSV template, then add your data to the exported file and re-import it
- Use **Merge** mode when adding new records to an existing dataset
- Use **Replace** mode only when you want to completely reset the app's data

pages.title: Creating a Forms App
pages.body:
When you create a new workspace with a Forms App included, RacerX automatically opens a **Forms Editor** tab. This is where you design your app before it goes live.

The Forms Editor tab has a purple top border to distinguish it from regular app tabs. You can switch to other tabs at any time and come back to the editor — it stays open until you close it yourself.

**Choosing a name and icon**

At the top of the editor, give your app a name and pick an icon from the emoji picker. The name and icon appear in the left sidebar once the app is deployed.

**Choosing a template**

Select a starting point from the template gallery:

- **Blank** — start with an empty app and define your own fields later
- **CRM** — Contacts, Companies, and Deals tables pre-built for customer relationship management
- **Issue Tracker** — a single Issues table with status, priority, assignee, and due date
- **Wedding Planner** — Guests, Vendors, and Checklist tables for event planning

Templates are starting points. You can customize any template further using the SQL Viewer once the app is deployed.

**Deploying your app**

Click **Deploy** to create the database tables and make the app available to all workspace members. The Forms Editor tab stays open so you can make notes, but the app is now live.

**AI Generate**

For something completely custom, select the **AI Generate** tile instead of a template. AI Generate has two modes:

- **Quick Create** — describe your app in a few sentences and click **Generate & Deploy**. The AI reads your description, designs the tables and fields, and deploys the app in one step.

- **Ask Questions** — instead of generating immediately, the AI asks you a series of clarifying questions: What will this app track? What fields matter most? What status values do you need? When you are satisfied with the design, click **Deploy** and the AI builds the schema from your conversation.

**Choosing an AI provider**

A provider selector lets you choose between Claude, OpenAI, and Gemini. All three can design a Forms App schema — selecting different providers is a good way to compare results and pick the design you prefer. The provider you choose must have an API key configured in Settings.

**Quick Create vs Ask Questions — which to use**

Use Quick Create when you have a clear picture of your app and want a fast result. Use Ask Questions when you are still figuring out the structure — the conversation helps you think through the fields, relationships, and status values before anything is built.

Either way, a well-designed schema saves time later. It is much easier to plan the right fields up front than to restructure data after records have been created.

pages.title: AI Schema Editor
pages.body:
The AI Schema Editor is a conversational assistant for modifying the structure of an existing Forms App — adding or removing tables and fields, adjusting types and options, and wiring up lookup relationships.

**Opening the AI assistant**

In the Schema tab of the Forms Editor, click the **✨ AI** button in the toolbar. The AI panel slides in on the right. Click **✨ AI** again to close it. You can drag the divider between the editor and the panel to resize both.

**Choosing a provider**

Select Claude, OpenAI, or Gemini at the top of the panel. A provider is only selectable if you have configured an API key for it in **Manage → API Keys**.

**How it works**

Describe what you want to change in plain English. The AI asks 1–3 clarifying questions at a time until it understands the request. When it has enough information it will say so and invite you to say **"go"** — or you can say "go" at any point to stop the questions and begin.

Once you say "go" (or the AI is fully confident), it generates a list of schema operations and applies them to the editor immediately. You will see the tables and fields update in real time.

**Multi-batch schema changes**

For complex requests — building a full CRM, redesigning a schema from scratch — the AI splits its work into multiple batches. Each batch is a group of related operations applied together. Here is how the chain works:

1. **You send a prompt.** Your message, the full conversation history, and the current in-memory schema are sent to the AI.
2. **The AI responds.** It either asks a clarifying question, or sends an operations batch — a structured list of changes to make.
3. **The batch is applied.** The panel shows "Batch N of M — [summary]" and applies each operation to the schema in the editor. You see the tables and fields update in real time.
4. **If more batches remain**, the panel automatically sends "continue" to the AI. The AI picks up where it left off and sends the next batch.
5. **When all batches are done**, you see "✓ Done — N batches applied. Review the schema, then click Save." The schema is updated in memory but **not saved to the database until you click Save**.

**Batch ordering and dependencies**

The AI is instructed to emit batches in dependency order: tables must exist before fields that reference them, and tables must exist before views that join them. Within each batch, operations are also ordered — a table is created before its fields are added. Earlier batches are generally a prerequisite for later ones.

**Each batch is atomic**

All operations in a batch are applied to the schema at once before the editor re-renders. If a single operation fails mid-batch (for example, referencing a table that does not yet exist), the preceding operations in that batch remain applied — there is no per-operation rollback. The Undo button rolls back the **entire batch** as a single step.

**Validation is on-demand, not per batch**

Validation does not run automatically between batches. Click **Validate** after the full run completes to check the final schema before saving.

**Undo**

An entire AI batch — however many operations it contains — counts as a single undo step. Press **⌘Z** (Mac) or **Ctrl+Z** (Windows) once to revert the whole batch. Individual operations within a batch cannot be selectively undone.

**Speed**

The Speed slider controls how fast the AI applies changes. At the leftmost position (Instant) all changes appear at once. Moving right slows down the animation so you can watch each field and table being added in sequence.

**Conversation history**

The conversation is saved automatically and reloads the next time you open the panel for the same app. Use the **Clear** button to wipe the history and start fresh.

**API costs — important**

The AI Schema Editor uses your own API key from the provider you have selected. All charges go directly to your account with that provider (Anthropic, OpenAI, or Google). RacerX does not charge for AI usage and never sees your billing details.

The panel header shows a running session total: tokens used and an estimated cost in USD. Each assistant reply also shows its individual token count and cost estimate.

Approximate pricing for the models used (as of mid-2025):

| Provider | Model | Input | Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Claude | Haiku 4.5 | $0.80 / 1M | $4.00 / 1M |
| OpenAI | GPT-4o mini | $0.15 / 1M | $0.60 / 1M |
| Gemini | 2.0 Flash | $0.075 / 1M | $0.30 / 1M |

These estimates are approximate. Actual charges depend on your provider tier, promotional credits, and any pricing changes the provider makes after this guide was written. Always verify current pricing on your provider's website.

**Controlling costs**

Each message you send includes the full conversation history as context. Costs increase as the conversation grows. To keep costs low:

- Use **Clear** between unrelated tasks to reset the context
- Be concise — a single well-written request costs less than several rounds of vague questions
- Say "go" as soon as the AI has enough information — extra clarification rounds add tokens
- Set a monthly spending limit with your provider before you start:
  - Anthropic: console.anthropic.com → Settings → Billing → Usage limits
  - OpenAI: platform.openai.com → Settings → Billing → Usage limits
  - Google: console.cloud.google.com → Billing → Budgets & alerts

pages.title: Schema Validation
pages.body:
The **Validate** button in the AI Assistant panel checks your schema for structural errors before you save or deploy.

**What it checks**

- Duplicate table or field IDs within the same schema
- IDs that are not valid snake_case (lowercase letters, digits, and underscores; must start with a letter or underscore)
- IDs that conflict with SQLite reserved words (such as `select`, `table`, `group`, `order`)
- Tables with no fields defined
- Lookup fields pointing to tables that do not exist
- Circular lookup chains (table A looks up table B which looks up table A)
- Select fields with no options defined
- Nav items pointing to tables that do not exist
- View joins referencing invalid tables

Warnings (non-blocking) are also shown for:

- Tables with only system fields and no user-defined fields
- Fields with blank labels
- Views with no fields selected

**Understanding cascading errors**

The validator reports every error it finds — not just the first one. However, some errors near the bottom of the list may be side effects of errors higher up. For example, if a table ID is invalid, every field and view that references that table will also produce an error.

Fix errors from the top of the list downward. After the AI applies a fix and you click Validate again, you may find that several lower errors have disappeared on their own.

**AI Fix**

Next to each error is an **AI Fix** button. Clicking it sends a targeted prompt to the AI asking it to resolve that specific issue. The validation panel stays visible while the AI works — you do not need to clear the results to continue the conversation.

**Dismiss**

Click **Dismiss** next to any error or warning you want to remove from the list without fixing it. Dismissing an item does not change the schema — it only hides the item from view in the current session. The next time you click Validate, all issues are re-evaluated from scratch.

pages.title: SQL Viewer — Overview
pages.body:
The SQL Viewer lets you query your RacerX data directly using SQL. It is a read-only tool — you cannot modify data through it.

**Accessing the SQL Viewer:**

Click **SQL Viewer** in the tab bar at the top of the app.

**Interface layout:**

- **Tables panel (left)** — lists all available tables grouped by workspace and app; click any table name to populate the query input with a default `SELECT * FROM … LIMIT 100`
- **SQL | AI toggle** — switches the input between SQL mode (write queries by hand) and AI mode (describe what you want in plain English)
- **Query input (bottom)** — type your SQL or description here
- **Run / Generate button** — in SQL mode, executes the query; in AI mode, sends your description to the AI and generates SQL. Keyboard shortcut: **⌘Enter** (Mac) or **Ctrl+Enter** (Windows)
- **Results area (main panel)** — shows the history of queries run this session, each with column headers, rows, and a row count
- **Copy as Report** — copies the current query formatted as a wiki report block, ready to paste into any wiki page
- **Download CSV** — saves the most recent result set as a CSV file
- **Clear** — clears the session history
- **⚙ Settings** — opens the AI API key dialog; turns purple when a key is configured

**Restrictions:**

Only `SELECT` statements are permitted. `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, `DROP`, `ALTER`, and `CREATE` return an error.

**Collapsing the tables panel:**

Click the **‹** icon at the top of the tables panel to hide it and give the query area more space.

pages.title: SQL Viewer — AI Mode
pages.body:
AI mode lets you describe what you want to query in plain English. The AI generates the SQL for you — you review it and press Run to execute.

**Getting started — API key required:**

AI mode requires your own API key from an AI provider (Anthropic Claude, OpenAI, or Google Gemini). Each user brings their own key; charges go to your AI provider account directly. RacerX never sees your key except to forward it to the provider's API.

1. Get an API key from your chosen provider
2. In the SQL Viewer, click the **⚙** gear icon
3. Paste your key and click **Save**

The gear icon turns purple once a key is saved.

**Using AI mode:**

1. Click the **AI** segment in the SQL | AI toggle
2. Type a plain-English description — for example: *show me all open issues assigned to Rick*
3. Press **Generate** (or ⌘Enter / Ctrl+Enter)
4. The AI generates a SQL SELECT and places it in the input box, switching to SQL mode automatically
5. Review the query, then press **Run** to execute

**How the AI understands your data:**

When you press Generate, RacerX sends the AI a compact description of your database schema — table names and column names — along with your question. The AI never sees your actual data, only the structure.

**Tips for good results:**

- Be specific: mention filter conditions, sort order, and row limits when relevant
- Reference data by concept — *messages*, *wiki pages*, *open issues* — rather than raw table names
- If the result is not what you expected, toggle back to AI, refine your description, and Generate again
- Check the generated SQL before running it

pages.title: SQL Viewer — Database Structure
pages.body:
RacerX stores your data in a local SQLite database. Table names include the application ID, which is visible in the Tables panel on the left.

**Messenger tables:**

- `channels_{appId}` — id, workspace_id, name, created_by, created_at, is_archived
- `messages_{appId}` — id, channel_id, sender_id, sender_name, body, created_at, edited_at, is_deleted, edit_of
- `reactions_{appId}` — id, message_id, user_id, emoji, created_at

**Wiki tables:**

- `wiki_categories_{appId}` — id, name, created_at
- `wiki_pages_{appId}` — id, category_id, title, body, created_by, created_at, edited_at

**Forms App tables:**

Forms Apps use dynamic table names based on the app ID and the field schema defined in the app's `schema.json`. The general pattern is:

- `records_{appId}` — one row per record; columns vary by app schema
- `upload_queue` — pending cloud uploads (managed internally; read-only)
- `sync_log` — history of sync operations (managed internally; read-only)

To see the exact column names for a Forms App, click the app's table name in the Tables panel — the prefilled SELECT query shows all columns.

**Timestamps:**

All `created_at`, `edited_at`, and `created` columns store Unix timestamps in milliseconds. To display them as human-readable dates:
```sql
datetime(created_at / 1000, 'unixepoch', 'localtime')
```

pages.title: SQL Viewer — Sample Queries
pages.body:
Use these queries as starting points. Click any table name in the Tables panel to get a prefilled SELECT with the correct table name.

**List all wiki pages with category:**
```sql
SELECT c.name as category, p.title,
       datetime(p.created_at / 1000, 'unixepoch', 'localtime') as created
FROM wiki_pages_{appId} p
JOIN wiki_categories_{appId} c ON c.id = p.category_id
ORDER BY c.name, p.title;
```

**Recent messages with sender names:**
```sql
SELECT sender_name, body,
       datetime(created_at / 1000, 'unixepoch', 'localtime') as sent_at
FROM messages_{appId}
WHERE is_deleted = 0
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

**Count messages per channel:**
```sql
SELECT c.name, COUNT(m.id) as message_count
FROM channels_{appId} c
LEFT JOIN messages_{appId} m ON m.channel_id = c.id AND m.is_deleted = 0
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY message_count DESC;
```

**Search message content:**
```sql
SELECT sender_name, body,
       datetime(created_at / 1000, 'unixepoch', 'localtime') as sent_at
FROM messages_{appId}
WHERE body LIKE '%search term%' AND is_deleted = 0
ORDER BY created_at DESC;
```

**Check sync log for recent activity:**
```sql
SELECT app_id, direction, status, file_path,
       datetime(ts / 1000, 'unixepoch', 'localtime') as at
FROM sync_log
ORDER BY ts DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

**Pending uploads:**
```sql
SELECT id, app_id, record_id,
       datetime(created_at / 1000, 'unixepoch', 'localtime') as queued_at
FROM upload_queue
ORDER BY created_at ASC;
```

pages.title: SQL Viewer — Report Blocks
pages.body:
The SQL Viewer and Wiki work together through Report Blocks — a way to embed live SQL query results directly in wiki pages.

**Creating a report block from the SQL Viewer:**

1. Write and run a query in SQL mode
2. Verify the results are what you want
3. Click **Copy as Report** in the SQL Viewer header
4. The query is copied to the clipboard, wrapped in the report block syntax:
````
```report
Your SQL here
```
````
5. Open a wiki page, place the cursor where you want the report, and paste

**The `{app}` token:**

Copy as Report automatically replaces the raw app ID in the table name with `{app}`. This makes the report portable — it works correctly in any workspace without editing the SQL.

For example, if your query was:
```sql
SELECT title FROM wiki_pages_abc123 ORDER BY title
```
After Copy as Report it becomes:
```sql
SELECT title FROM wiki_pages_{app} ORDER BY title
```

**What makes a good report block:**

- Queries with a small, stable set of columns (wide tables are hard to read inline)
- Queries that return 5–50 rows (very large results are hard to scan)
- Queries with meaningful `ORDER BY` and `LIMIT` clauses
- Avoid joins with many tables — keep report SQL simple and readable

pages.title: Sync Dashboard — Overview
pages.body:
The Sync Dashboard shows the status of all sync jobs running on this device — uploads, downloads, and workspace supervisors. Access it by clicking **Sync** in the left sidebar.

**Job types:**

- **Upload** — one per Forms App; queues record saves, CSV imports, and baseline publishes and sends them to cloud storage
- **Download** — one per Forms App; polls cloud storage for new records from other devices and applies them to your local database
- **Supervisor** — one per workspace; handles workspace-level tasks (app discovery, member metadata); runs manually only

**The job table:**

Each row represents one job. The columns are:

| Column | Description |
|---|---|
| Name | App name and job type (Upload / Download) |
| Workspace | Which workspace the app belongs to |
| Status | idle / syncing / paused / error |
| Last Run | Timestamp of the most recent poll or upload; shows record count or an error indicator |
| Next Run | Scheduled time for the next automatic poll; “Manual only” for Supervisor rows |
| Interval | Foreground / background interval (e.g. “5 min / 30 min”) |

**Controls:**

- **▶ Run** — trigger an immediate sync poll (not available for manual-only jobs)
- **⏸ Pause / ▶ Resume** — pause or resume scheduled sync (workspace owners only); persists across restarts
- **↺ Reset** — available on Download rows only; see the **Resetting a Download Job** page
- **+ / −** — expand or collapse the sync log for this job

**The sync log:**

Click **+** on any Upload or Download row to expand a log of recent sync events for that job — records applied, records uploaded, errors, and timestamps.

**The colored dot in the sidebar:**

The Sync nav item shows a small dot next to the label:
- ● green — all jobs are healthy
- ● red — at least one job is in an error state

The dot is a quick-glance indicator; open the dashboard to see which job is erroring and why.

**Pausing sync:**

Upload and download jobs can be paused independently. Pausing upload means new saves queue locally and are sent when you resume — no data is lost. Pausing download stops the polling timer; records from other devices accumulate in cloud storage and are applied in bulk when you resume.

Owners can pause their own device’s jobs. Non-owners see status and history but cannot change sync settings.

pages.title: Resetting a Download Job
pages.body:
The **↺ Reset** button appears on Download job rows in the Sync Dashboard. It clears this device’s download cursor for that app and immediately triggers a fresh download from cloud storage.

**What happens when you reset:**

1. The download cursor for the app is cleared — the device forgets where it left off
2. A sync poll runs immediately
3. If a baseline file exists in cloud storage, it is applied first (a full snapshot of all records)
4. All individual record files written after the baseline are applied on top, in order

**What is preserved:**

Local changes that have not yet been uploaded are never overwritten. Local always wins when the local version is newer. Only records that do not exist locally, or records where the cloud version is newer, are applied.

**When to use Reset:**

- **Recovering missing data** — if records from another device are not appearing after a manual Run, Reset forces a complete re-download from scratch
- **Simulating a new device** — use during testing to verify that a new team member would receive the correct dataset
- **Cleaning up after a bad import** — if a CSV import created records with missing or invalid IDs, Reset re-pulls from cloud storage; only properly formed records (uploaded after the issue was corrected) will be applied, giving you a clean local copy
- **Troubleshooting sync errors** — if a job is stuck in an error state and a manual Run does not recover it, Reset is the next step

**Confirmation step:**

Clicking ↺ Reset shows a confirmation prompt before proceeding: “Reset cursor? Yes / No”. This is intentional — resetting re-downloads the full dataset for that app, which may take a moment for large datasets.

**Reset only affects this device:**

Resetting a download job has no effect on cloud storage or on other team members’ devices. It only changes what this device considers “already downloaded.”

pages.title: Managing Your Workspace
pages.body:
**Workspace roles:**

Each member of a workspace has a role:
- **Owner** — can invite members, delete the workspace, create and delete apps, and access all administrative features
- **Editor** — can read and write all data but cannot manage members or delete the workspace
- **Viewer** — read-only access (coming soon)

**Inviting members:**

Workspace owners share the workspace folder through the cloud provider's sharing interface. The invited person will see the shared workspace in their workspace list on next launch.

**Removing a member:**

Remove the person's access to the shared folder through your cloud provider's sharing settings.

**Workspace ownership:**

Ownership can be transferred to another member. Contact the current owner to initiate a transfer.

**Deleting a workspace:**

Only the owner can delete a workspace. Deletion removes the workspace folder and all its data from cloud storage. This cannot be undone.

**Your role while signed out:**

Signed out of Dropbox or OneDrive, you're still the owner of the apps you own there: they stay on **Manage Apps → Owner**, marked **Signed out**, and don't sync until you sign in again. See **Support → Frequently Asked Questions**.

pages.title: Your Account
pages.body:
**Viewing account info:**

Click the cloud provider icon at the bottom-left of the sidebar to open your account panel. It shows your display name and email address as provided by your cloud storage account.

**Signing out:**

Click **Sign out** in the account panel. You will be taken back to the sign-in screen. Your cloud data is not deleted when you sign out.

**Signing back in:**

Click **Sign in with Dropbox** (or your cloud provider) on the sign-in screen. After authorizing, all your workspaces and data reappear and sync resumes automatically.

**Trial period:**

RacerX is available on a trial basis. All features are available during the trial. Purchasing details will be provided before the trial expires.

pages.title: Platform Architecture
pages.body:
RacerX uses a three-layer native shell architecture. Each platform has its own thin native shell that hosts a WebView running the React UI. The React UI communicates with a Node.js backend process over localhost HTTP. The backend owns all I/O: SQLite, cloud storage API calls, and credential management.

```mermaid
graph TD
    subgraph macOS
        MA[Swift NSApplication]
        MW[WKWebView]
        MN[Bundled Node.js v22]
    end
    subgraph Windows
        WA[C# WinForms]
        WW[WebView2 Edge]
        WN[System Node.js ARM64]
    end
    subgraph Ubuntu
        UA[GTK4 Application]
        UW[WebKitGTK WebView]
        UN[System Node.js]
    end
    MA --> MW
    MA --> MN
    WA --> WW
    WA --> WN
    UA --> UW
    UA --> UN
    MN & WN & UN --> BE[Node.js Backend\nExpress HTTP — localhost]
    BE --> DB[(SQLite\nLocal database)]
    BE --> CS[Cloud Storage API\nDropbox / OneDrive]
    MW & WW & UW -.->|HTTP fetch| BE
```

**Layer 1 — Native shell**

The shell creates the application window, starts the Node.js backend as a child process, and hosts the WebView. It has no business logic. Its only jobs are window management, menu bar, and bridging the OS lifecycle (wake from sleep, foreground/background transitions) to the backend via WebView messages.

- **macOS**: Swift / NSApplication / WKWebView. Node.js is bundled inside the .app bundle at `Contents/Resources/node`. Backend starts before the WebView loads. Shell detects backend readiness by polling the health endpoint.
- **Windows**: C# / WinForms / WebView2. Uses the system-installed Node.js (ARM64 on Parallels/Surface). Backend stdout and stderr are redirected to `%APPDATA%\racerx\node.log`. WebView2 user data folder is at `RacerX.exe.WebView2\` next to the executable.
- **Ubuntu**: GTK4 / WebKitGTK. Architecturally identical to macOS; shell code is in `ubuntu-shell/`.

**Layer 2 — Node.js backend**

An Express HTTP server on a dynamically-assigned localhost port. Handles all persistence and cloud API calls. Key responsibilities:

- SQLite read/write (better-sqlite3)
- Dropbox and OneDrive REST API calls
- OAuth2 token management (keychain / kv.js file fallback)
- Sync engine: upload queue processor, download poller, baseline publisher
- Wiki seed loading at startup
- WebSocket broadcast for real-time sync notifications

The backend is started by the shell with the port number as an environment variable. The React UI receives the port via an injected `window.RACERX_PORT` global.

**Layer 3 — React SPA**

A Vite-built React app served from `web-ui/dist/` (production) or Vite dev server (local dev). Communicates with the backend exclusively via `fetch()` to localhost. Has no direct disk or network access.

**Zero-server guarantee**

The backend runs entirely on the user's device. No RacerX server exists. All cloud traffic goes from the user's device directly to Dropbox or OneDrive APIs using the user's own OAuth credentials.

pages.title: Data Architecture
pages.body:
RacerX uses two storage layers: a local SQLite database on each device and JSON files in cloud storage.

**Local SQLite database**

One database file per device. All reads from the UI go through this database, so the app feels fast and works offline.

The backend opens two connections to the same file:
- `dbRW` — read-write connection (INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE); used by all write operations
- `db` — read-only connection; used by SELECT queries; opened *after* dbRW creates the file

The file is opened exclusively by the Node.js process. The shell never touches it directly.

Database paths:

| Platform | Default path |
|---|---|
| macOS | `~/Library/Application Support/com.example.racerx/racerx.db` |
| Windows | `%APPDATA%\racerx\racerx.db` |
| Ubuntu | `~/.local/share/com.example.racerx/racerx.db` |

The path can be overridden with the `DB_PATH` environment variable (used by the shell to pass an explicit path on Windows).

**Core tables (always present)**

- `workspaces` — registered workspaces: id, name, root_path, cloud_provider, member_role, owner_email
- `upload_queue` — pending cloud uploads: id, app_id, record_id, payload JSON, created_at
- `sync_log` — history of sync events: direction, status, file_path, error, ts
- `sync_cursors` — per-app download cursors: app_id, cursor value
- `deleted_workspace_paths` — prevents re-adding ejected workspaces
- `ai_conversations` — AI Schema Editor conversation history per app

**App tables (created dynamically)**

When a Forms App is deployed, its tables are created from `schema.json`:
- `records_{appId}` — one row per record; columns match the app's field schema
- For Messenger: `channels_{appId}`, `messages_{appId}`, `reactions_{appId}`
- For Wiki: `wiki_categories_{appId}`, `wiki_pages_{appId}`

**Cloud storage — record format**

Each record is stored as a separate JSON file in cloud storage. A typical record file looks like:

```json
{
  "id": "rec_01HX...",
  "app_id": "app_abc123",
  "table": "records_app_abc123",
  "data": {
    "name": "Acme Corp",
    "status": "active",
    "created_at": 1748000000000
  },
  "updated_at": 1748000000000,
  "deleted": false
}
```

Timestamps are Unix milliseconds throughout. `deleted: true` records are tombstones — applying them removes the record from the local table.

**Last-write-wins conflict resolution**

If two devices write the same `record_id` simultaneously, the file with the higher `updated_at` wins when the other device downloads it. No merge, no diff. This is intentional — it is simple and predictable for the append-heavy workflows RacerX targets (new CRM contacts, new messages, new wiki pages).

pages.title: Sync Engine
pages.body:
The sync engine has two independent loops per Forms App: an **upload loop** and a **download loop**. Each runs on its own timer. A workspace-level **supervisor** handles workspace metadata (app discovery, member info) and runs manually.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    participant UI as React UI
    participant BE as Node.js Backend
    participant DB as SQLite
    participant CS as Cloud Storage

    Note over UI,BE: Write path (immediate)
    UI->>BE: POST /forms/save-record
    BE->>DB: INSERT/UPDATE record row
    BE->>DB: INSERT upload_queue row
    BE-->>UI: 200 OK (record appears instantly)

    Note over BE,CS: Upload loop (every 5 min foreground)
    loop Upload queue drain
        BE->>DB: SELECT oldest upload_queue row
        BE->>CS: PUT {tsMs}_{uuid}.json
        BE->>DB: DELETE upload_queue row
        BE->>DB: INSERT sync_log (upload, ok)
    end

    Note over BE,CS: Download loop (every 5 min foreground)
    loop Poll for new files
        BE->>CS: LIST records since cursor
        CS-->>BE: new file paths
        BE->>CS: GET each new file
        BE->>DB: INSERT/UPDATE record rows
        BE->>DB: UPDATE sync_cursor
        BE->>DB: INSERT sync_log (download, ok)
    end
```

**Upload loop**

1. Upload queue processor fires on a timer (foreground: 5 min; background: 30 min).
2. Reads the oldest `upload_queue` row.
3. Uploads the payload JSON to `{recordsPath}/{tsMs}_{uuid}.json` in cloud storage.
4. Deletes the queue row on success; writes a `sync_log` error row on failure.
5. Repeats until the queue is empty.

Uploads are fire-and-retry — if the upload fails, the queue row remains and is retried on the next timer tick.

**Download loop**

1. Download poller fires on the same timer as the upload loop.
2. Reads the stored cursor for this app from `sync_cursors`.
3. Lists cloud storage files in the `records/` folder written after the cursor position.
4. Downloads each new file, parses the JSON, and applies it to the local SQLite table.
5. Advances the cursor to the newest file position.
6. Applies tombstone files from the `tombstones/` folder separately.

**Cursor semantics**

The cursor is an opaque value returned by the cloud provider's list API (a Dropbox cursor or OneDrive `$skipToken`). It encodes "give me everything after this point." Resetting a cursor (via the ↺ Reset button in Sync Dashboard) clears it to null, forcing a full re-download from the beginning of the folder.

**Baseline**

For large datasets, a workspace owner can publish a `baseline.json` — a single file containing all current records as a JSON array. A new device receiving the workspace applies the baseline first, then applies individual record files written after the baseline was published. This avoids downloading N individual files.

**Foreground vs background**

The sync engine receives `tab:active` / `tab:inactive` messages from the React UI and adjusts timer intervals accordingly. Foreground interval: 5 minutes. Background interval: 30 minutes. The app also fires an immediate poll on `app:wake` (device waking from sleep) and when a new app is added to the workspace.

**Supervisor**

The supervisor runs manually (no automatic timer). It handles:
- App discovery: scans the workspace `apps/` folder in cloud storage and registers any unrecognised apps
- Member metadata sync: fetches display names and avatar URLs from the cloud provider sharing API

Trigger it via the **▶ Run** button on the Supervisor row in the Sync Dashboard.

pages.title: Authentication & Credentials
pages.body:
RacerX uses OAuth2 to authenticate with Dropbox and OneDrive. The user's credentials never pass through RacerX — authentication happens entirely between the user's browser and the cloud provider.

**OAuth2 flow**

1. User clicks "Sign in with Dropbox" (or OneDrive) in the React UI.
2. React UI tells the Node.js backend to start the OAuth flow.
3. Backend opens a localhost redirect server on an ephemeral port.
4. Backend opens the cloud provider's authorization URL in the user's default browser (via the native shell's `openURL` bridge).
5. User approves access in the browser.
6. Cloud provider redirects to `http://localhost:{port}/callback` with an authorization code.
7. Backend exchanges the code for an access token + refresh token.
8. Backend stores the tokens via `kv.js`.

**Token storage — kv.js**

`backend/src/sync/kv.js` is a thin wrapper that tries the system keychain first and falls back to a plain JSON file.

| Platform | Primary storage | Fallback |
|---|---|---|
| macOS | System keychain (Security framework via keytar) | `~/.racerx/kv.json` |
| Windows | Windows Credential Manager (via keytar) | `~/.racerx/kv.json` |
| Ubuntu | libsecret (via keytar) | `~/.racerx/kv.json` |

On Windows ARM64 (Parallels), `keytar` has no prebuilt binary for `win32-arm64`. The `require('keytar')` call is wrapped in `try/catch` — the error is logged but not fatal. All credential operations fall through to the JSON file at `~/.racerx/kv.json` (i.e. `C:\Users\{user}\.racerx\kv.json`). This file is created with mode `0o600` (owner-read-write only on POSIX platforms).

**Token refresh**

Access tokens expire (Dropbox: 4 hours; OneDrive: 1 hour). Before any cloud API call, the backend calls `getValidAccessToken()`, which checks expiry and refreshes if needed. A mutex (single-flight lock) prevents concurrent refreshes — if two async operations trigger a refresh simultaneously, only one HTTP call is made; the second waits for the result.

**Keychain prompts on macOS**

On the first launch, or after an app update, macOS may show a keychain access dialog: "RacerX wants to use the login keychain." Click **Always Allow**. This is a one-time prompt per app version. If denied, the token cannot be stored and sign-in will not persist across restarts.

**Sign-out**

Sign-out clears the in-memory token, removes the keychain entry (or kv.json entry), and clears all workspace/session data from the React UI's localStorage. The SQLite database is not deleted — local data persists until the user does a manual reset.

pages.title: Cloud Storage Layout
pages.body:
All RacerX data in cloud storage lives under a single root folder. The root folder name is controlled by the `CLOUD_ROOT` constant in `backend/src/cloud-paths.js`. Current value: `RacerX` (accessed via the API as `/racerx` in Dropbox path conventions).

**Folder tree**

```
/racerx/                                         ← CLOUD_ROOT (all-lowercase in API paths)
  {workspace-slug}/                              ← workspacePath(name)
    _rx_meta.json                                ← workspace owner, display name, created_at
    apps/
      {appId}/
        schema.json                              ← field definitions, views, nav config
        {App Name}.txt                           ← human-readable app name (empty file)
        _rx_app_meta.json                        ← app type, display name
        PROD/
          records/
            {tsMs}_{uuid}.json                   ← individual record files
            {tsMs}_bulk_{uuid}.json              ← bulk import files (CSV → cloud)
            baseline.json                        ← full snapshot (owner-published)
          tombstones/
            {tsMs}_{uuid}_deleted.json           ← delete markers (soft deletes)
```

**Notes on naming**

- `{workspace-slug}` is the workspace name lowercased with URL-unsafe characters replaced by dashes. Example: "Acme Corp" → `acme-corp`.
- `{appId}` is a short random ID generated at app creation (e.g. `a1b2c3d4`).
- Record file names: `{tsMs}_{uuid}.json` — Unix millisecond timestamp + UUID. The timestamp prefix makes files sortable chronologically by name, which is how the download cursor advances.
- `PROD` is the environment segment. A `DEV` environment is reserved for future use (schema migrations, staging).

**`_rx_meta.json`**

Written by the workspace creator. Contains:
```json
{
  "owner": "user@example.com",
  "displayName": "Acme Corp",
  "created_at": "2026-05-01T12:00:00Z"
}
```
Used by invited members to identify the workspace owner. Never modified after creation (ownership transfer is a future feature).

**schema.json**

The app's field and view definitions. Example minimal schema:
```json
{
  "tables": [
    {
      "id": "contacts",
      "label": "Contacts",
      "fields": [
        { "id": "name", "label": "Name", "type": "text" },
        { "id": "email", "label": "Email", "type": "text" }
      ]
    }
  ]
}
```

**What is NOT in cloud storage**

- The SQLite database (device-local only)
- User preferences (localStorage, device-local)
- OAuth tokens (keychain or kv.json, device-local)
- The `node_modules` folder (never synced)
- The React build output (included in the app bundle)

**Path migration note**

Before App Store submission, `CLOUD_ROOT` will be changed from `RacerX` to a final name (task #22 / #10). All path construction derives from this one constant in `cloud-paths.js`. No other files need changing.

pages.title: Build System & Native Modules
pages.body:
Each platform has its own build script. All three produce the same runtime: native shell → Node.js backend → React SPA in WebView.

**macOS**

Build script: `macos-shell/build.sh`

1. Checks that the bundled Node.js version matches the `better-sqlite3` binary ABI.
2. Runs `npm ci` in `web-ui/` and `npm run build` to produce `web-ui/dist/`.
3. Copies `assets/wiki_seed.json` → `backend/src/server/wiki_seed.json`.
4. Builds the Xcode project (Swift) via `xcodebuild`.
5. Launches the resulting `.app`.

The bundled Node.js lives at `macos-shell/RacerX/node` and is included in the Xcode target. It is the same binary that runs the backend at runtime. This ensures the native module ABI (`process.versions.modules`) is always consistent — the binary that compiled `better-sqlite3` is the same binary that loads it.

**Windows**

Build script: `windows-shell/build.ps1`

1. Pulls `git reset --hard origin/main`.
2. If dependencies are missing, calls `setup.ps1` to install Node.js, Python, and .NET 8 SDK via `winget` and `fnm`.
3. Prepends `C:\Program Files\nodejs` to PATH before running `npm install` in `backend/`. This is critical on ARM64 machines where `fnm` installs an x64 Node.js that shadows the system ARM64 Node.js. Native module lifecycle scripts (`prebuild-install`) must see `process.arch = 'arm64'` to download the correct prebuilt binary.
4. Runs `npm install --prefer-offline` in `web-ui/` and `npm run build`.
5. Builds the C# project via `dotnet build`.
6. Launches `RacerX.exe`.

See **Windows ARM64 Notes** in the Support section for details on the native module issue.

**Ubuntu**

Build script: `ubuntu-shell/build.sh`

Structurally identical to macOS. Uses the system Node.js, GTK4, and WebKitGTK. First-time setup: `ubuntu-shell/setup.sh`.

**Native modules**

Two native modules require platform-specific binaries:

| Module | Purpose | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| `better-sqlite3` | SQLite driver | Prebuilt binaries available for all platforms including win32-arm64 |
| `keytar` | OS keychain access | No win32-arm64 prebuilt; kv.js file fallback used on Windows ARM64 |

If `better-sqlite3` loads an ABI-mismatched binary, the backend crashes immediately with "invalid ELF header" (Linux) or "not a valid Win32 application" (Windows). Fix: delete `backend/node_modules` and run `build.ps1` / `build.sh` (the PATH fix in `build.ps1` ensures the correct ARM64 binary is downloaded).

**Vite dev server (macOS/Ubuntu — UI-only iteration)**

```bash
cd web-ui
PATH="/opt/homebrew/Cellar/node/25.9.0_2/bin:$PATH" npm run dev
```

Opens `http://localhost:5173`. The running backend (started by the shell) serves API calls. Use this for rapid UI changes without a full Xcode/dotnet rebuild.

pages.title: Frequently Asked Questions
pages.body:
**What happens to my apps when I sign out of Dropbox or OneDrive?**

While you're signed out of Dropbox or OneDrive, the apps you own there stay on the **Owner** tab of **Manage Apps**, marked **Signed out**. In the sidebar their storage icon is greyed.

Nothing is lost, but nothing syncs either: changes you make, including owner tasks from the app's **⋮** menu such as Sharing or Publish Baseline, can't reach the cloud until you sign in again. Click **Signed out** (or the Dropbox or OneDrive icon at the bottom of the sidebar) to sign in.

If you sign in to a *different* Dropbox or OneDrive account, apps owned by the first account move to **Read-Write**, because that account isn't the owner.

Apps on this device only, on a network share or in iCloud Drive don't depend on signing in.

pages.title: Storage Locations
pages.body:
This page documents exactly where RacerX stores data on each platform. Knowing these locations is essential for clean resets, backups, and diagnosing issues.

**macOS**

The macOS app runs in an App Sandbox. The actual data directory depends on which bundle ID is in use. The shell searches these candidate paths in order and uses the first one that contains a `racerx.db` file:

| Priority | Path |
|---|---|
| 1 (current dev build) | `~/Library/Containers/com.racerx.racerx/Data/Library/Application Support/com.racerx.racerx/racerx.db` |
| 2 (new bundle ID)     | `~/Library/Containers/com.example.racerx/Data/Library/Application Support/com.example.racerx/racerx.db` |
| 3 (non-sandboxed fallback) | `~/Library/Application Support/com.example.racerx/racerx.db` |

To see which path is actually in use, check for the presence of a racerx.db file in each location. In practice the development Xcode build uses `com.racerx.racerx` (inherited from the Flutter era).

| What | Notes |
|---|---|
| SQLite database | In the Container listed above |
| OAuth tokens | System keychain — search "RacerX" in Keychain Access |
| WebKit / localStorage | Also inside the sandbox container |
| Backend logs | Xcode console or Console.app (no persistent log file) |

**Windows**

| What | Path |
|---|---|
| SQLite database | `%APPDATA%\racerx\racerx.db` |
| OAuth tokens | `%USERPROFILE%\.racerx\kv.json` (keytar fallback on ARM64) |
| Backend stdout + stderr | `%APPDATA%\racerx\node.log` |
| localStorage / WebView2 prefs | `windows-shell\bin\Debug\net8.0-windows\RacerX.exe.WebView2\` |

The WebView2 folder is next to `RacerX.exe` in the build output. It stores everything the Edge WebView2 engine persists: localStorage (`rx_theme`, session data), IndexedDB, cookies. **This folder is NOT inside `%APPDATA%\racerx`** and is not deleted by the standard reset command.

**Ubuntu**

| What | Path |
|---|---|
| SQLite database | `~/.local/share/com.example.racerx/racerx.db` |
| OAuth tokens | libsecret keyring (or `~/.racerx/kv.json` fallback) |
| localStorage / WebKitGTK prefs | `~/.local/share/com.example.racerx/` |

**Cloud storage**

Your RacerX data in the cloud lives at `/racerx/` inside your Dropbox or OneDrive account root. It is accessed exclusively via the provider's API — it does NOT appear in your local Dropbox or OneDrive sync folder. To browse files directly, use the provider's web interface (dropbox.com, onedrive.live.com).

pages.title: Reset Procedures — macOS
pages.body:
Use this procedure to reset RacerX on macOS to a clean state — as if it were a first launch.

**What a full reset does**

- Removes the local SQLite database (all locally cached data)
- Removes OAuth tokens from the keychain (forces re-authentication)
- Clears localStorage and WebView state (resets theme, session)

**What it does NOT do**

- Does not delete cloud storage data (your Dropbox/OneDrive files are untouched)
- Does not delete `node_modules` (no rebuild needed after a reset)

**Step 1 — Quit the app**

Make sure RacerX is not running.

**Step 2 — Delete the app data**

The macOS app is sandboxed. The database and all WebKit storage live inside a Containers folder — NOT in the standard `~/Library/Application Support/`. Delete the `Data/` subdirectory inside each container (the container root itself is OS-managed and cannot be deleted):

```bash
rm -rf ~/Library/Containers/com.racerx.racerx/Data/
rm -rf ~/Library/Containers/com.example.racerx/Data/
rm -rf ~/Library/Application\ Support/com.example.racerx/
rm -rf ~/.racerx/
```

Do **not** attempt `rm -rf ~/Library/Containers/com.racerx.racerx/` — macOS protects `.com.apple.containermanagerd.metadata.plist` at the container root and the command will fail with "Operation not permitted."

**Step 3 — Remove keychain entries**

```bash
security delete-generic-password -s "RacerX" 2>/dev/null; true
```

Or open **Keychain Access** (Applications → Utilities), search for "RacerX", and delete any entries.

**Step 4 — Relaunch**

```bash
open ~/Library/Developer/Xcode/DerivedData/RacerX-*/Build/Products/Debug/RacerX.app
```

On first launch after a reset, you will be prompted to sign in again.

**Bundle ID note**

The current development build uses bundle ID `com.racerx.racerx` (carried over from the Flutter era). Before App Store submission, this will be changed to a final identifier (task #10). At that point the container path will change and this procedure must be updated to match. The shell's candidate list in `AppDelegate.buildNodeEnvironment()` must also be kept in sync.

pages.title: Reset Procedures — Windows
pages.body:
Use this procedure to reset RacerX on Windows to a clean state — as if it were a first launch.

**What a full reset does**

- Removes the local SQLite database and backend log
- Removes stored OAuth credentials (kv.json)
- Clears WebView2 localStorage and session state (resets theme preference, etc.)

**What it does NOT do**

- Does not delete cloud storage data (your Dropbox/OneDrive files are untouched)
- Does not delete `node_modules` or rebuild the app (no rebuild needed after a data reset)

**Run these commands in PowerShell:**

```powershell
# Remove database, log, and backend data
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:APPDATA\racerx" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

# Remove OAuth credentials (kv.json fallback)
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "$env:USERPROFILE\.racerx" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue

# Remove WebView2 storage — includes localStorage (rx_theme, session data)
# This folder is next to the built exe, NOT inside AppData
Remove-Item -Recurse -Force "windows-shell\bin\Debug\net8.0-windows\RacerX.exe.WebView2" -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue
```

Run from the repo root (`C:\projects\racerx-git` or wherever you cloned the repo).

**After a reset, relaunch normally:**

```powershell
.\windows-shell\build.ps1
```

On first launch after a reset, you will be prompted to sign in again.

**Why the WebView2 folder matters**

The React UI stores user preferences in the browser's `localStorage`. This includes `rx_theme` (dark/light mode). The WebView2 engine stores `localStorage` in `RacerX.exe.WebView2\` — not in `%APPDATA%\racerx`. If you only delete the AppData folder, localStorage survives and the app may appear to launch in a state that seems pre-configured. Always delete both folders for a true clean state.

**If node_modules are corrupt**

If the app crashes on startup with a message about `better-sqlite3`, the native binary may be mismatched. Delete `backend\node_modules` and run `build.ps1` — it will reinstall with the correct ARM64 prebuilt. See **Windows ARM64 Notes** for details.

pages.title: Windows ARM64 Notes
pages.body:
RacerX on Windows runs on ARM64 hardware (e.g. Parallels on Apple Silicon, or a Surface Pro X/11). This page documents the native module requirements and the known issue with `fnm`.

**The problem: two Node.js binaries, wrong architecture**

Native Node.js modules (`.node` files) are compiled for a specific CPU architecture. An x64 `.node` file cannot be loaded by an ARM64 `node.exe`, and vice versa — the OS refuses to load it ("not a valid Win32 application").

On a typical Windows ARM64 machine with `fnm` (Fast Node Manager) installed:
- `C:\Program Files\nodejs\node.exe` — **ARM64** (the OS-installed version, v24+)
- `~\AppData\Roaming\fnm\node-versions\v22\...\node.exe` — **x64** (fnm always installs x64 on ARM64 Windows)

`fnm` activates itself by inserting its directory early in `$PATH`. This means `node` in a PowerShell session resolves to fnm's x64 binary.

When `npm install` runs `better-sqlite3`'s install script (`prebuild-install`), it uses the bare `node` from PATH — NOT npm's co-located node. It sees `process.arch = 'x64'` and downloads the x64 prebuilt binary. When the app launches using the system ARM64 node, it tries to load the x64 binary and crashes.

**The fix (in build.ps1 and setup.ps1)**

Before every `npm install` in the `backend/` directory, the build scripts prepend the system node directory to PATH:

```powershell
$env:PATH = "$env:ProgramFiles\nodejs;$env:PATH"
$sysNpm = "$env:ProgramFiles\nodejs\npm.cmd"
if (Test-Path $sysNpm) { & $sysNpm install } else { try { npm install } catch { } }
```

This ensures `prebuild-install` sees `process.arch = 'arm64'` and downloads `node-v137-win32-arm64.tar.gz` (or equivalent).

**keytar — no ARM64 Windows prebuilt**

`keytar` (used for Windows Credential Manager access) has no prebuilt binary for `win32-arm64` at any Node.js module version. The `require('keytar')` call in `backend/src/sync/kv.js` is wrapped in a `try/catch`. If keytar fails to load, a warning is printed and all credential operations fall through to the JSON file fallback at `~\.racerx\kv.json`. The app functions normally.

**Verification**

To verify that the correct binary is loaded:

```powershell
# Check node architecture
& "$env:ProgramFiles\nodejs\node.exe" -e "console.log(process.arch)"
# Expected: arm64

# Check better-sqlite3 loads
& "$env:ProgramFiles\nodejs\node.exe" -e "require('./backend/node_modules/better-sqlite3'); console.log('OK')"
# Expected: OK
```

If the second command prints "FAIL: not a valid Win32 application", delete `backend\node_modules` and run `build.ps1` to reinstall with the correct binary.

pages.title: Diagnostic Tools
pages.body:
Use these tools to investigate sync, data, and startup issues.

**SQL Viewer**

The SQL Viewer tab provides direct read-only access to the local SQLite database. Key diagnostic queries:

Check pending uploads:
```sql
SELECT id, app_id, record_id,
       datetime(created_at / 1000, 'unixepoch', 'localtime') as queued_at
FROM upload_queue ORDER BY created_at ASC;
```

Check recent sync activity:
```sql
SELECT direction, status, file_path, error,
       datetime(ts / 1000, 'unixepoch', 'localtime') as at
FROM sync_log ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 30;
```

Check all registered workspaces:
```sql
SELECT id, name, cloud_provider, member_role, root_path FROM workspaces;
```

Check download cursors:
```sql
SELECT * FROM sync_cursors;
```

**Backend log — Windows**

The Node.js backend's stdout and stderr are captured to:
```
%APPDATA%\racerx\node.log
```

Open in any text editor. The log is overwritten on each launch. If the app crashes on startup, this file contains the error. Common crash signatures:

- `Error: SQLITE_CANTOPEN` — database directory does not exist; run reset procedure
- `Error: not a valid Win32 application` loading `better-sqlite3` or `keytar` — ARM64/x64 mismatch; delete `backend\node_modules` and run `build.ps1`
- `Error: listen EADDRINUSE` — a previous Node.js process did not exit; kill it in Task Manager

**Backend log — macOS**

On macOS the backend runs as a child process of the Swift shell. Stdout/stderr appear in the Xcode console when launched via Xcode, or in Console.app (search for "racerx") when launched from the .app. There is no persistent log file on macOS — attach Xcode or use Console.app for diagnostics.

**Sync Dashboard**

The Sync Dashboard (Sync tab in the sidebar) shows real-time sync status. Expand any job row with **+** to see per-file sync events. Red dot in the nav = at least one job is in error state.

**WebView DevTools**

On macOS: right-click anywhere in the RacerX window and choose **Inspect Element** (requires `defaults write com.example.racerx WebKitDeveloperExtras -bool true` to enable). The full Safari Web Inspector appears.

On Windows: enable DevTools by adding `--remote-debugging-port=9222` to the Node.js start command (in `MainForm.cs`). Then navigate to `chrome://inspect` in a Chromium-based browser.

pages.title: Messages Not Appearing
pages.body:
If messages sent on one device are not appearing on another:

1. **Check the polling interval** — Messenger polls every 15 seconds in the foreground. Wait up to 15 seconds after sending.

2. **Verify both apps are connected** — Both devices need an active internet connection and valid cloud storage authentication.

3. **Use the SQL Viewer to verify** — Run `SELECT * FROM messages_{appId} ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5` on the receiving device. If the message is not there, it has not been downloaded yet. If it is there but not showing in the UI, that is a display issue.

4. **Restart the app** — A full restart forces a fresh sync from the beginning.

pages.title: Wiki Pages Not Updating
pages.body:
If a wiki page saved on one device is not appearing on another:

1. **Check that RacerX is open and in the foreground** — The Wiki polls cloud storage every 5 minutes. The receiving device must have RacerX open and active.

2. **Wait up to 5 minutes** — Changes will appear within that window once the app is in the foreground.

3. **Verify with the SQL Viewer** — Run `SELECT title, datetime(edited_at / 1000, 'unixepoch', 'localtime') as edited FROM wiki_pages_{appId} ORDER BY edited_at DESC` on the receiving device. If the page does not appear or shows an old edit time, it has not synced yet.

4. **Restart the app** — A full restart forces an immediate poll.

pages.title: Forms Data Not Syncing
pages.body:
If records added or edited on one device are not appearing on another:

1. **Wait up to 5 minutes** — Forms sync every 5 minutes in the foreground.

2. **Check the upload queue** — In the SQL Viewer, run:
```sql
SELECT id, app_id, record_id, datetime(created_at / 1000, 'unixepoch', 'localtime') as queued
FROM upload_queue ORDER BY created_at ASC;
```
If rows appear here, the records have been written locally but not yet uploaded. This is normal for a few minutes after editing. If rows persist for more than 10 minutes, check your internet connection.

3. **Check the sync log** — In the SQL Viewer, run:
```sql
SELECT direction, status, file_path, error,
       datetime(ts / 1000, 'unixepoch', 'localtime') as at
FROM sync_log ORDER BY ts DESC LIMIT 20;
```
Errors in this log indicate what went wrong during a sync attempt.
